questions.text: BPH most commonly arises from which zone of the prostate?
questions.explanation: BPH develops in the transitional zone, whereas prostate cancer arises predominantly (70–80%) from the peripheral zone.

questions.text: In uncomplicated bladder outflow obstruction due to BPH, which finding is typical?
options: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
originalOptions: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.correctAnswer: D) Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.correctAnswerText: Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.explanation: A maximum flow rate below 15 mL/sec (with <10 mL/sec strongly suggestive) is typical of obstruction. Finasteride takes 6+ months to work, and alpha-blockers (not agonists) relieve symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT assessed by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)?
questions.explanation: IPSS assesses seven voiding/storage symptoms (incomplete emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, nocturia) but does not include incontinence, As a key word (FUN II SS) frequency,urgency,nocturnal , incomplete empathy,intermittent,stream is weak ,straining

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of the voiding (obstructive) phase in BPH?
questions.explanation: Frequency is a storage symptom. Voiding/obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, weak stream, straining, intermittency, and terminal dribbling.

questions.text: Which symptom is NOT related to urine storage phase dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Weak stream is a voiding (obstructive) phase symptom. Storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has an IPSS of 22 (severe). What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 blockers such as terazosin are first-line medical therapy for BPH, even with severe IPSS scores. Surgery is reserved for failed medical therapy or complications.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT used in the treatment of BPH?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 agonists cause smooth muscle contraction and would worsen bladder outflow obstruction. Beta-blockers also have no established role in BPH, but alpha-agonists are the classically incorrect option since they directly oppose the mechanism of alpha-blocker therapy.

questions.text: Tamsulosin, used in the treatment of BPH, acts as a(n):
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin is a selective alpha-1A antagonist that relaxes prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle to improve urinary flow.

questions.text: Which of the following is an indication for open (simple) prostatectomy rather than TURP?
options: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
originalOptions: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
questions.correctAnswer: A) Prostate size greater than 80 grams
questions.explanation: A prostate weighing more than 80 g is generally too large for safe transurethral resection (increased TUR syndrome risk), making open (or laparoscopic/robotic) simple prostatectomy preferable.

questions.text: Which statement about anticholinergic drugs in BPH is FALSE?
options: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
originalOptions: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
questions.correctAnswer: B) They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
questions.correctAnswerText: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics are contraindicated, not indicated, when PVR exceeds 150 mL, due to the risk of precipitating acute urinary retention.

questions.text: Antimuscarinic therapy for LUTS/BPH is contraindicated:
options: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
originalOptions: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
questions.correctAnswer: A) Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
questions.correctAnswerText: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinics are contraindicated specifically in men with large, persistent PVR due to retention risk; they can safely be combined with alpha-blockers for mixed storage and voiding symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic medications?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation (not diarrhea), along with dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized side effect of tamsulosin?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin's known side effects are retrograde ejaculation (most common), postural hypotension, and rhinitis/nasal congestion; decreased libido is not a typical alpha-blocker side effect.

questions.text: Regarding post-void residual (PVR) assessment in BPH, which statement is most accurate?
options: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
originalOptions: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
questions.correctAnswer: A) PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
questions.correctAnswerText: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
questions.explanation: PVR is typically measured using ultrasound (avoiding invasive catheterization) and should be assessed in patients with significant voiding symptoms or before certain interventions, though it is not measured after every single void.

questions.text: Which symptom is LEAST specific for bladder outflow obstruction?
questions.explanation: Nocturia can result from many causes (polyuria, cardiac disease, aging) besides bladder outflow obstruction, making it the least specific symptom among the choices.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a storage symptom of BPH?
questions.explanation: Dysuria reflects pain during urination (typically from inflammation) and is not a standard storage LUTS; storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT occur during the voiding phase?
questions.explanation: Nocturia is a storage-phase symptom, while hesitancy and weak stream are voiding-phase symptoms.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with LUTS has IPSS 22 and PVR 50 mL. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.explanation: With a severe IPSS but only mildly elevated PVR and no indication for surgery, first-line medical therapy with an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) is appropriate.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has IPSS symptom score of 22, PVR 50 cc, prostate volume 60 cc, severe detrusor instability on cystometrogram, and high-grade obstruction on pressure-flow study. The best next step to improve symptoms is:
questions.explanation: Despite urodynamic evidence of obstruction and detrusor overactivity, initial management remains medical therapy with an alpha-blocker before considering surgery, given no absolute surgical indication is present.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man on tamsulosin and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for 2 months continues to have obstructive symptoms. The next step is:
options: Continue current therapy and reassess later
originalOptions: Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.correctAnswer: B) Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.correctAnswerText: Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors require at least 6 months to show clinical benefit; persistent symptoms after only 3 months, without complications, warrant continued therapy and reassessment rather than surgery.

questions.text: Tamsulosin combined with a PDE5 inhibitor should be used with caution due to the risk of:
questions.explanation: Both alpha-blockers and PDE5 inhibitors cause vasodilation; their combination increases the risk of significant hypotension.

questions.text: Which bladder tumor originates from the urachus?
questions.explanation: Urachal remnants at the bladder dome give rise to adenocarcinoma, often presenting with mucusuria. TCC and SCC arise from urothelium and chronic irritation respectively, not urachal remnants.

questions.text: Which type of bladder cancer is caused due to chronic irritation?
questions.explanation: Chronic irritation (Schistosoma, long-term catheterization, bladder stones, recurrent UTI) causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, progressing to SCC over time.

questions.text: Which of the following environmental factors is highly associated with bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Smoking accounts for roughly half of bladder cancers, conferring a 2–6× increased risk via carcinogenic arylamines. Occupational and radiation exposure are recognized risk factors but contribute far less overall.

questions.text: Typical presentation of bladder cancer:
questions.explanation: This is the classic presentation, seen in 80–85% of patients, and represents total hematuria from the bladder. Irritative symptoms like frequency or dysuria are less common and suggest CIS.

questions.text: 68-year-old male patient diagnosed with bladder TCC; on TURBT histology came back as T2 bladder TCC. Best next treatment option is:i
questions.explanation: T2 disease invades the muscularis propria, defining muscle-invasive bladder cancer, which requires radical cystectomy (± neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy). Intravesical therapies are reserved for non-muscle-invasive disease.

questions.text: Which is considered the best for follow-up of bladder cancer after resection?
questions.explanation: Cystoscopy is the gold standard for surveillance, allowing direct visualization and biopsy of recurrent lesions. Imaging modalities lack the sensitivity to detect small mucosal recurrences.

questions.text: Which one of the following intravesical treatments CANNOT be given immediately after bladder cancer resection?
questions.explanation: Intravesical chemotherapy (such as Mitomycin) can be administered as a single dose within 24 hours of resection to eliminate circulating tumor cells. However, intravesical BCG (an attenuated strain of mycobacteria) must be delayed for at least 2 weeks post-resection. This delay allows the resection site to heal completely, preventing potentially fatal systemic mycobacterial dissemination and BCG-sepsis.

questions.text: High-grade bladder tumor characteristics:
questions.correctAnswer: A) High progression AND high recurrence
questions.explanation: High-grade tumors carry both high recurrence and high progression risk, whereas low-grade tumors have high recurrence but low progression potential.

questions.text: A 62-year-old male presents with intermittent, painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a papillary bladder tumor, and he undergoes a complete transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). The final histopathology report confirms a Ta, low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the immediate management of this patient?
questions.explanation: A single immediate instillation post-TURBT reduces recurrence by ~50% in Ta low-grade tumors. BCG is reserved for T1, CIS, or high-grade Ta disease due to its higher toxicity.

questions.text: Egyptian man with previous Schistosoma parasite infection — most common bladder cancer type:
questions.explanation: S. haematobium is endemic in Egypt; eggs deposited in the bladder wall trigger chronic inflammation and squamous metaplasia, leading to SCC rather than TCC.

questions.text: Risk factor for bladder cancer from occupation:
questions.explanation: Aromatic amines such as benzidine and beta-naphthylamine are established occupational carcinogens in these industries, as well as in painting and hairdressing.

questions.text: What is the definitive treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion is the gold standard for T2+ disease. Chemotherapy alone and intravesical therapy are inadequate once muscularis propria is invaded.

questions.text: Which group is more affected by bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Male:female ratio is roughly 3:1, with peak incidence at 60–70 years; smoking further amplifies this predominant demographic risk.

questions.text: Which of the following is a risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines in the rubber industry is a well-established, strong risk factor. Family history confers only a modest (two-fold) increase in comparison.

questions.text: Patient with uncontrolled HTN, colon cancer treated with cyclophosphamide + radiotherapy, now has invasive bladder cancer — what is LEAST likely to increase bladder cancer risk?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is not a recognized bladder cancer risk factor, whereas cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiotherapy, and smoking are all established causative agents.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder?
questions.explanation: Eggs lodging in the bladder wall provoke chronic granulomatous inflammation and squamous metaplasia, culminating in SCC — unlike ordinary bacterial UTIs.

questions.text: 60-year-old smoker with painless intermittent gross hematuria. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswer: A) TCC (transitional cell carcinoma) bladder cancer
questions.explanation: TCC accounts for ~90% of bladder cancers and is strongly linked to smoking, presenting classically with painless intermittent gross hematuria.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Alcohol has no established causal link to bladder cancer, unlike smoking, occupational carcinogen exposure, and male gender, which are all recognized risk factors.

questions.text: Most common cancer associated with persistent urachus:
questions.explanation: A persistent urachal remnant at the bladder dome predisposes to adenocarcinoma, distinct from the urothelium-derived TCC affecting the rest of the bladder.

questions.text: Patient with bladder cancer stage T1, high risk for progression, underwent resection; after 2 weeks what is the next step?
questions.explanation: High-risk T1 tumors require re-resection (repeat TURBT) to exclude understaging or residual disease before committing to intravesical therapy.

questions.text: Patient treated with BCG has a biopsy showing CIS with muscle invasion. What is the best management?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion
questions.explanation: Muscle invasion signifies progression beyond the scope of intravesical therapy; BCG failure with invasive disease mandates radical cystectomy.

questions.text: Patient found to have bladder cancer; after TURBT the histology came back as T1. What is the next step?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Cystoscopy follow-up and intravesical therapy
questions.explanation: T1 tumors are non-muscle-invasive, so management consists of surveillance cystoscopy with intravesical instillation rather than radical surgery.

questions.text: The most common presentation of bladder cancer:
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria is the classic and most common presenting symptom, seen in the majority of bladder cancer patients.

questions.text: Urine cytology is most sensitive for?
options: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
originalOptions: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.correctAnswer: B) High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.correctAnswerText: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.explanation: Urine cytology detects poorly differentiated cells shed from high-grade tumors and CIS with high sensitivity, but often misses well-differentiated low-grade lesions.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a component of trimodal therapy for bladder-preserving treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Trimodal therapy combines maximal TURBT with concurrent chemotherapy and radiotherapy specifically to spare the bladder; radical cystectomy is the alternative it aims to avoid.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the classical presentation of bladder cancer, particularly when carcinoma in situ is present?
options: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
originalOptions: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
questions.correctAnswer: C) Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
questions.correctAnswerText: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
questions.explanation: Classic presentation is painless intermittent hematuria; irritative symptoms suggest CIS.

questions.text: Which chemotherapeutic agent is itself a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Its urotoxic metabolite (acrolein) damages the urothelium, increasing bladder cancer risk.

questions.text: A low-risk non-muscle-invasive tumor is resected. Most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: A single post-TURBT instillation reduces recurrence in low-risk disease without BCG-level toxicity.

questions.text: A high-risk T1, high-grade tumor is found after TURBT. Recommended intravesical therapy?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Induction BCG followed by maintenance
questions.explanation: High-risk T1/high-grade or CIS requires induction BCG plus maintenance for optimal recurrence/progression control.

questions.text: Which finding after TURBT mandates repeat TURBT?
options: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
originalOptions: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.correctAnswer: B) T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.correctAnswerText: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.explanation: These carry understaging risk, so repeat TURBT confirms true depth of invasion before further treatment.

questions.text: A patient has very-high-risk or BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. Best management?
questions.explanation: BCG-unresponsive or very-high-risk disease carries high progression risk, favoring cystectomy over further intravesical salvage.

questions.text: Which correctly differentiates timing of chemotherapy vs. BCG after TURBT?
options: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
BCG within 24 hours; chemotherapy delayed 2 weeks
originalOptions: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
BCG within 24 hours; chemotherapy delayed 2 weeks
questions.correctAnswer: B) Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
questions.correctAnswerText: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
questions.explanation: Immediate chemo reduces recurrence; BCG needs intact urothelium to avoid systemic dissemination.

questions.text: An IVU during the bladder-filling phase shows a radiolucent filling defect. Most likely diagnosis? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: A radiolucent filling defect on IVU most commonly represents a urothelial tumor projecting into the lumen.

questions.text: Given a radiolucent bladder filling defect on IVU, which is LEAST likely as a differential? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: Pyelonephritis is a renal parenchymal infection and does not cause a bladder filling defect.

questions.text: A radiolucent bladder filling defect is seen with hematuria. Next step? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
options: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
originalOptions: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
questions.correctAnswer: B) Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
questions.correctAnswerText: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
questions.explanation: TURBT gives histological diagnosis and staging; cytology/imaging are adjuncts, not substitutes.

questions.text: This imaging study was performed during the bladder-filling phase, showing a radiolucent filling defect. What is the name of this imaging study? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: IVU uses IV contrast excreted by the kidneys to opacify the collecting system, ureters, and bladder, allowing detection of filling defects such as tumors.

questions.text: Regarding urological imaging studies, what is the most important risk of exposure to ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation from CT and fluoroscopic urological studies carries a cumulative risk of carcinogenesis, making malignancy induction the most clinically significant long-term hazard. Skin irritation and cataracts require far higher cumulative doses to manifest. ## All of the following are true about kidney anatomy, EXCEPT: A) An oval intraperitoneal organ B) Left kidney has a longer renal vein C) Right kidney is smaller than the left kidney D) Kidneys are bean-shaped structures E) Kidneys are bilateral structures Correct Answer: A) An oval intraperitoneal organ Explanation: Kidneys are retroperitoneal, bean-shaped structures, not intraperitoneal. The right kidney sits lower and is often described as slightly smaller, while the left renal vein is longer as it crosses the aorta to reach the IVC.

questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE about kidney anatomy?
options: Kidneys lie posterior in the abdomen
originalOptions: Kidneys lie posterior in the abdomen
questions.explanation: Kidneys lie retroperitoneally against the posterior abdominal wall, not within the peritoneal cavity. All other listed features (bilateral, bean-shaped, posterior location) accurately describe renal anatomy.

questions.text: The correct order of the division of the intrarenal branches of the renal artery is:
questions.explanation: The renal artery branches sequentially from segmental arteries into interlobar arteries running between pyramids, then arcuate arteries arching at the corticomedullary junction, and finally interlobular arteries ascending into the cortex.

questions.text: The only segment of the urethra that does NOT have transitional epithelium is the:
questions.explanation: The fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, distinguishing it from the transitional epithelium lining the more proximal urethral segments listed as options. Another way to phrase the question: Which segment is lined by stratified squamous epithelium? Ans: E.

questions.text: Ultrasound has many advantages which include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: It is safe and does not use ionizing radiation
It requires little or no pre-procedural preparation
It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
It can be safely performed in pregnant women
It is not affected by renal function
originalOptions: It is safe and does not use ionizing radiation
It requires little or no pre-procedural preparation
It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
It can be safely performed in pregnant women
It is not affected by renal function
questions.correctAnswer: C) It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
questions.correctAnswerText: It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is limited in differentiating pseudotumors from true renal lesions; CT or MRI are superior for this characterization. Its safety, minimal preparation, and independence from renal function are genuine advantages.

questions.text: Which of the following is associated with suprapubic pain?
questions.explanation: Bladder pathology such as cystitis or overdistension classically produces suprapubic discomfort, whereas renal colic and ureteric stones typically cause flank pain radiating to the groin.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding physical examination?
options: The testes in men should be the same size
The normal prostate is the size of a walnut
A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
It is best to examine a man's genitalia in a warm room
originalOptions: The testes in men should be the same size
The normal prostate is the size of a walnut
A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
It is best to examine a man's genitalia in a warm room
questions.correctAnswer: D) A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
questions.correctAnswerText: A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
questions.explanation: A "bag of worms" texture describes a varicocele, not a hydrocele; a hydrocele is a smooth, fluid-filled swelling that transilluminates. A warm room helps relax the cremasteric reflex for accurate examination.

questions.text: All the following can cause a DECREASE in specific gravity of urine EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dehydration concentrates the urine, raising specific gravity, whereas increased fluid intake, diuretics, and impaired concentrating ability all dilute urine and lower specific gravity.

questions.text: Which of the following are used in the calculation of plasma osmolarity?
questions.explanation: Plasma osmolarity is estimated as 2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, incorporating sodium as the main osmotic contributor along with glucose and urea.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about renal pain?
options: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
originalOptions: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
questions.explanation: Renal pain arises from capsular distension, with inflammatory pain being steady while obstructive pain fluctuates; it can also mimic intraperitoneal pathology, though patients with renal pain classically prefer to move (rolling sign) unlike those with peritoneal pain.

questions.text: Choose the WRONG statement about kidney anatomy:
options: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
Left kidney is higher than the right
Right kidney extends from 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
Left kidney extends from 12th thoracic to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
The right kidney is displaced inferiorly by the liver
originalOptions: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
Left kidney is higher than the right
Right kidney extends from 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
Left kidney extends from 12th thoracic to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
The right kidney is displaced inferiorly by the liver
questions.correctAnswer: A) Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
questions.correctAnswerText: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
questions.explanation: The right kidney actually lies 1-2 cm lower than the left due to the liver's position above it, making the left kidney the higher of the two.

questions.text: Choose the WRONG statement:
options: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
Obstruction causes colicky pain and inflammation causes steady pain
Renal colic fluctuates in intensity as the kidney attempts to relieve obstruction
Steady inflammatory pain reflects capsular distension without peristaltic surges
Obstructive pain fluctuates due to ureteral peristalsis against the blockage
originalOptions: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
Obstruction causes colicky pain and inflammation causes steady pain
Renal colic fluctuates in intensity as the kidney attempts to relieve obstruction
Steady inflammatory pain reflects capsular distension without peristaltic surges
Obstructive pain fluctuates due to ureteral peristalsis against the blockage
questions.correctAnswer: A) Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
questions.correctAnswerText: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
questions.explanation: This reverses the actual pattern: inflammatory renal pain is steady, while obstructive pain fluctuates in intensity as the ureter undergoes hyperperistalsis to overcome the blockage.

questions.text: Radiographically, the ureter is divided into how many parts?
questions.explanation: The ureter is anatomically and radiologically divided into upper, middle (over the sacrum), and lower segments, corresponding to abdominal, pelvic, and intramural portions.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs does NOT cause renal failure?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used for bladder outlet obstruction and lacks nephrotoxic potential, unlike ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, and NSAIDs, which can impair renal perfusion or cause direct tubular injury.

questions.text: Which imaging modality is safest for a patient in renal failure?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound requires no contrast or radiation exposure and is unaffected by renal function, making it the safest imaging choice in renal impairment, unlike iodinated or gadolinium-based contrast studies which risk nephrotoxicity or nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

questions.text: Renal pain classically radiates to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain radiates from the flank toward the groin and may be referred to the testis due to shared T11-T12 innervation, distinguishing it from intraperitoneal pain, which classically radiates to the shoulder.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the male urethra from proximal to distal?
questions.explanation: The male urethra begins at the bladder neck, passing through the prostatic segment, then the membranous urethra at the external sphincter, followed by the bulbar and pendulous penile urethra ending at the fossa navicularis.

questions.text: A patient presents with flank pain. Which feature would favor a urological (renal) rather than an intraperitoneal cause?
options: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
originalOptions: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
questions.correctAnswer: C) Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
questions.correctAnswerText: Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
questions.explanation: Renal colic patients characteristically move restlessly (rolling sign) due to colicky pain, whereas intraperitoneal pathology causes steady pain with patients preferring to remain motionless.

questions.text: Pneumaturia is best defined as which of the following?
options: Presence of gas in the urine
Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine
originalOptions: Presence of gas in the urine
Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine
questions.correctAnswer: B) Presence of gas in the urine
questions.correctAnswerText: Presence of gas in the urine
questions.explanation: Pneumaturia results from recent catheterization, an enteric fistula, or infection with gas-forming organisms, distinguishing it from hematuria (blood) or enuresis (nocturnal incontinence).

questions.text: Which of the following is a FALSE statement about gonadal veins?
options: The right gonadal vein terminates in the inferior vena cava below the level of the right renal vein
The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava
The left gonadal vein has a longer course than the right before reaching its terminal vessel
The right gonadal vein is more prone to reflux-related pathology than the left despite its shorter course
Varicocele is more common on the left side than the right
originalOptions: The right gonadal vein terminates in the inferior vena cava below the level of the right renal vein
The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava
The left gonadal vein has a longer course than the right before reaching its terminal vessel
The right gonadal vein is more prone to reflux-related pathology than the left despite its shorter course
Varicocele is more common on the left side than the right
questions.correctAnswer: B) The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava
questions.correctAnswerText: The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava
questions.explanation: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein rather than the IVC directly, giving it a longer, higher-pressure course that predisposes to left-sided varicocele; the right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC.

questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation presents with new-onset gross hematuria and mild flank discomfort, with no fever or dysuria. What is the best initial investigation?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation and contrast, making it the safest first-line imaging choice in pregnancy for evaluating hematuria.

questions.text: One of the following is true about the prostate:
options: It secretes the majority of seminal fluid volume
originalOptions: It secretes the majority of seminal fluid volume
questions.explanation: A is correct — the prostate secretes zinc, citric acid, and PSA. B is wrong because fructose is a seminal vesicle product. C is wrong; albumin is not a prostatic secretion. D is wrong because the seminal vesicles, not the prostate, contribute the majority of seminal fluid volume. E is wrong; testosterone is produced by the testis, not the prostate.
