Essential investigations: urine culture and complete blood count; Causes: dehydration, excessive fluid intake, and diuretic use
Essential investigations: serum PSA and testosterone level; Causes: hydrocele, varicocele, and epididymitis
Essential investigations: 24-hour urine collection and renal biopsy in all cases; Causes: nocturnal polyuria, urgency, and frequency
Essential investigations: uroflowmetry and post-void residual; Causes: bladder outlet obstruction, prostatic enlargement, and urethral stricture
questions.correctAnswer: A) Essential investigations: cystoscopy and upper tract imaging; Causes: urinary tract stones, urothelial/renal malignancy, glomerular disease
questions.correctAnswerText: Essential investigations: cystoscopy and upper tract imaging; Causes: urinary tract stones, urothelial/renal malignancy, glomerular disease
questions.explanation: Hematuria in an adult is malignancy until proven otherwise, so cystoscopy assesses the bladder while upper tract imaging evaluates the kidneys and ureters, with stones, malignancy, and glomerular disease as the key causes to exclude. The distractors instead describe irritative symptom workup, scrotal pathology, or bladder outlet obstruction assessment, none of which target hematuria evaluation.

questions.text: All of the following are appropriate questions to ask when taking a history of hematuria EXCEPT:
options: Is the blood present at the start, throughout, or at the end of the urinary stream?
Is the hematuria associated with pain, or is it painless?
Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
originalOptions: Is the blood present at the start, throughout, or at the end of the urinary stream?
Is the hematuria associated with pain, or is it painless?
Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.correctAnswer: E) Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: Timing of blood in the stream, presence or absence of pain, clot characteristics, and smoking or occupational exposure history are all directly relevant to localizing and risk-stratifying hematuria, whereas morning stiffness is a rheumatological question unrelated to urological assessment.

questions.text: All of the following are irritative LUTS symptoms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hesitancy is an obstructive symptom reflecting delayed initiation of urination, whereas frequency, urgency, nocturia, and dysuria are all irritative symptoms related to bladder storage and mucosal irritation.

questions.text: A 68-year-old man reports voiding 10 times during the day and waking up 3 times at night to urinate, each time passing only a small volume, with a strong sudden desire to void that is difficult to defer. His total 24-hour urine output is normal. Which category of symptoms best describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: Frequency, nocturia with small voided volumes, and urgency despite a normal total daily urine output point to decreased functional bladder capacity or mucosal irritation, characteristic of irritative rather than obstructive symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes true hematuria from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: Dipstick is positive for blood in all three conditions, but only true hematuria shows intact red blood cells on microscopic urinalysis.

questions.text: A patient reports blood appearing only at the very end of the urinary stream, after most of the urine has already passed. This pattern of terminal hematuria most suggests pathology arising from:
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bladder neck or prostatic inflammation
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria localizes to the urethra, total hematuria to the bladder or upper tract, and terminal hematuria to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra.

questions.text: A 68-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless gross hematuria. Which diagnosis must be excluded first as the classic cause of painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 years old?
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, warranting cystoscopy and upper tract imaging regardless of other findings.

questions.text: A normotensive patient is found to have isolated microscopic hematuria on routine urinalysis, with no other urinary symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate initial action?
questions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria in a low-risk patient is initially managed conservatively with a repeat urinalysis rather than immediate invasive workup.

questions.text: When taking a history from a patient presenting with hematuria, which combination of questions is most important to ask?
questions.explanation: Onset, presence of clots, and timing during the urinary stream all help localize the source and severity of hematuria, so all should be asked.

questions.text: Hematuria in an adult should be treated as a warning sign of which of the following until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Although hematuria has many causes, it is classically taught that hematuria in an adult signals malignancy, most often bladder cancer, until excluded.

questions.text: A 70-year-old male smoker presents with gross hematuria persisting for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
questions.explanation: Persistent gross hematuria in an older smoker requires full evaluation of both the upper tract (CT urogram) and lower tract (cystoscopy) to exclude urothelial malignancy.

questions.text: Which statement about carcinoma of the prostate is correct?
options: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
originalOptions: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
questions.correctAnswer: B) It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
questions.correctAnswerText: It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer is an adenocarcinoma graded by the Gleason score, arises predominantly in the peripheral zone, is hormone-dependent (responds to androgen deprivation therapy), and rarely invades the rectum due to Denonvilliers' fascia.

questions.text: What grading system is used for prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: The Gleason score assesses glandular architecture on low-power microscopy and correlates with prognosis; Bloom-Richardson is used for breast cancer, Breslow for melanoma, and Fuhrman for renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: PSA density is calculated as:
options: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
originalOptions: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
questions.correctAnswer: D) Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
questions.correctAnswerText: Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
questions.explanation: PSA density is total serum PSA divided by prostate volume (measured by TRUS); values above 0.15 ng/mL/g raise suspicion for malignancy.

questions.text: Serum PSA and digital rectal examination are primarily used for:
questions.correctAnswer: B) Early detection/screening for prostate cancer
questions.explanation: PSA testing combined with DRE is used for early detection of prostate cancer in asymptomatic men, though PSA is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific.

questions.text: Watchful waiting (as opposed to active surveillance) is most appropriate for men who:
options: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
originalOptions: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
questions.correctAnswer: C) Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
questions.correctAnswerText: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
questions.explanation: Watchful waiting is a palliative, symptom-directed strategy reserved for patients with limited life expectancy (≤10 years) and less aggressive disease, distinct from active surveillance which is used in younger, low-risk patients with curative intent.

questions.text: The most common site of prostate cancer metastasis is:
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer classically metastasizes to the axial skeleton, particularly the lumbar spine, producing osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions with associated back pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

questions.text: Which statement about the Gleason grading system is FALSE?
options: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
originalOptions: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
questions.correctAnswer: C) It does not correlate with prognosis
questions.correctAnswerText: It does not correlate with prognosis
questions.explanation: This statement is false — the Gleason score strongly correlates with prognosis and guides management decisions in prostate cancer.

questions.text: Serum PSA elevation may occur in association with which of the following?
questions.explanation: PSA is organ-specific, not disease-specific, and can be elevated by BPH, prostatitis, cancer, and mechanical manipulation of the prostate (e.g., catheterization, biopsy, DRE).

questions.text: Which is the most common cancer diagnosed in urology?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer diagnosed in men overall and the most common urological malignancy.

questions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has a Gleason score of 8 and PSA 25. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate management option?
questions.explanation: Active surveillance is reserved for low-risk disease; a Gleason score of 8 with PSA 25 indicates high-risk disease requiring definitive treatment such as surgery or radiotherapy with hormonal therapy.

questions.text: A patient with Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer is best managed with:
questions.explanation: Gleason 3+3 (grade group 1) represents low-risk disease, for which active surveillance is generally preferred to avoid overtreatment, provided other risk factors (PSA, stage, patient preference) support this approach.

questions.text: A patient has a suspicious prostatic mass on digital rectal exam with PSA of 9 ng/mL. The next step is:
questions.explanation: A suspicious DRE finding combined with elevated PSA warrants histological diagnosis via ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy rather than proceeding directly to surveillance or watchful waiting.

questions.text: All of the following are indications for prostate biopsy EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A high free:total PSA ratio (such as 30%) is reassuring and associated with a lower likelihood of cancer; a low ratio would instead raise suspicion and support biopsy.

questions.text: The Gleason score is used specifically for grading:
questions.explanation: The Gleason score is a histological grading system exclusively for prostate adenocarcinoma, based on glandular differentiation patterns.

questions.text: A patient with known advanced prostate cancer presents with new-onset back pain. The most appropriate immediate step is:
options: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
originalOptions: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.correctAnswer: D) Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.explanation: New back pain in a patient with known prostate cancer must first be evaluated for vertebral metastasis or spinal cord compression as an oncologic emergency; systemic androgen-deprivation therapy (GnRH/LHRH agonist) is appropriate for the underlying metastatic disease once red flags are excluded.

questions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has Gleason grade 8 and PSA greater than 20 with no metastatic findings on staging. Which management option is NOT appropriate?
questions.explanation: Active surveillance is unsuitable for high-risk, non-metastatic disease (Gleason 8, PSA >20); definitive treatment with surgery or radiotherapy plus hormonal therapy is indicated.

questions.text: After one year of therapy with a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, PSA typically:
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors reduce PSA levels by approximately 50% after 6–12 months of therapy; this must be accounted for when interpreting PSA values in patients on these drugs.

questions.text: What is the most common presentation of renal cell carcinoma?
options: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
originalOptions: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
questions.explanation: Most RCCs are now discovered incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons; the classic triad occurs in fewer than 10% of cases.

questions.text: What is the most common histopathological subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Clear cell RCC accounts for approximately 75% of RCC cases, is associated with VHL gene mutations, and carries the worst prognosis among the common subtypes.

questions.text: The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with RCC is:
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia, mediated via PTHrP secretion, is the most common paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with 2 months of painless visible hematuria, hypertension, weight loss, low-grade fever, and anemia. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Painless visible hematuria with hypertension and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fever, anemia) reflects the paraneoplastic and systemic presentation classically associated with renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: Renal cell carcinoma is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A vegetarian diet is not an established risk factor for RCC; recognized risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, long-term dialysis (ESRD), and inherited syndromes such as VHL disease.

questions.text: A patient presents with pneumothorax, cutaneous fibrofolliculomas, and a renal tumor. The most likely RCC subtype is:
questions.explanation: This triad is characteristic of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, which is associated with chromophobe/oncocytic renal tumors, skin fibrofolliculomas, and pulmonary cysts predisposing to pneumothorax.

questions.text: A patient has an RCC measuring 4 cm confined to the kidney. The preferred treatment is:
questions.explanation: Partial nephrectomy is preferred for T1 tumors (≤7 cm) when technically feasible, as it provides equivalent oncologic outcomes to radical nephrectomy while preserving renal function.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC?
questions.explanation: Increased serotonin is not a recognized paraneoplastic feature of RCC; recognized paraneoplastic syndromes include erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and Stauffer's syndrome (hepatic dysfunction without metastases).

questions.text: The classic triad of renal cell carcinoma consists of:
options: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
originalOptions: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.correctAnswer: D) Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.correctAnswerText: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.explanation: The classic (but now uncommon) triad of RCC is hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable flank mass, occurring together in less than 10% of patients.

questions.text: The most common site of RCC metastasis is:
questions.explanation: The lung is the most common site of metastasis for renal cell carcinoma, followed by bone and liver.

questions.text: Which of the following is an established risk factor for renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is a well-established risk factor for RCC, along with smoking, obesity, and long-term dialysis; alcohol and diabetes are not classically listed among the primary risk factors.

questions.text: Most cases of renal cell carcinoma are discovered:
questions.explanation: The majority of RCCs are detected incidentally during imaging performed for unrelated indications, reflecting the often silent early course of the disease.

questions.text: A patient with RCC presents with elevated hemoglobin (erythrocytosis). Which hormone is responsible?
questions.explanation: Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by the tumor causes paraneoplastic erythrocytosis in RCC; PTHrP causes hypercalcemia, not erythrocytosis.

questions.text: A 42-year-old Black male with known sickle cell disease is diagnosed with RCC. The most likely subtype is:
questions.explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait/disease and typically occurs in young Black patients, distinguishing it from the other subtypes.

questions.text: A patient is found to have a solid 4x5 cm renal mass in the lower pole. The next step in evaluation is:
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for characterizing a solid renal mass, as it allows assessment of enhancement (the key feature distinguishing RCC from benign lesions) and staging.

questions.text: A key imaging characteristic of tumors associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is:
questions.explanation: VHL-associated clear cell RCC tumors are characteristically hypervascular due to upregulation of angiogenic factors from loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene.

questions.text: Which of the following are established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma?
options: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
originalOptions: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
questions.explanation: ESRD, Smoking, obesity, and hypertension are all recognized, established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized paraneoplastic syndrome in RCC?
questions.explanation: Polycythemia (erythrocytosis) due to ectopic erythropoietin secretion is a well-recognized paraneoplastic syndrome of RCC; RCC is in fact the most common cause of paraneoplastic erythrocytosis

questions.text: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, nausea, bradycardia, and hypertension near the end of a prolonged resection. Serum sodium is low. This is best explained by:
options: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
originalOptions: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswer: A) Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswerText: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome results from absorption of hypotonic irrigating solution through open venous sinuses during resection, causing hypervolemic hyponatremia with confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and visual disturbances.

questions.text: Which factor is most associated with increased risk of TUR syndrome?
options: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
originalOptions: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Resection time greater than 90 minutes
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome risk increases with resection times exceeding 90 minutes and is more common in older men; bipolar TURP performed under saline (isotonic) irrigation reduces this risk.

questions.text: A patient requires long-term indwelling catheterization. Compared to latex, silicone catheters are preferred because they:
options: Are only available in smaller sizes
originalOptions: Are only available in smaller sizes
questions.explanation: Silicone catheters induce less tissue inflammation than latex, making them preferable for long-term catheterization, despite latex being cheaper and more widely available.

questions.text: A 24 French Foley catheter has an outer diameter of approximately:
questions.explanation: Catheter French size divided by 3 gives the outer diameter in millimeters; 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized indication for urethral catheterization?
options: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
originalOptions: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
questions.correctAnswer: A) Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
questions.correctAnswerText: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
questions.explanation: Monitoring urine output is a standard, common indication for catheterization. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, pelvic fracture with urethral disruption) is a contraindication until imaging excludes injury.

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to transurethral Foley catheter placement?
options: Need for a clean urine sample
originalOptions: Need for a clean urine sample
questions.explanation: Suspected urethral injury is a contraindication to urethral catheterization; a retrograde urethrogram should be performed first, and a suprapubic catheter used if drainage is needed.

questions.text: Chronic urinary retention is best distinguished from acute retention by which feature?
options: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
originalOptions: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
questions.correctAnswer: B) Painless, palpable, and percussible bladder
questions.explanation: Chronic retention classically presents as a painless, palpable/percussible bladder due to gradual distension, in contrast to the painful presentation of acute retention.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic heart disease presents with fever of 40°C, HR 125, BP 120/65, and suprapubic tenderness consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis with urinary retention. The most appropriate management is:
options: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
originalOptions: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
questions.correctAnswer: D) Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
questions.correctAnswerText: Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
questions.explanation: In acute bacterial prostatitis, urethral catheterization and instrumentation are contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia; urinary retention should be managed with a suprapubic catheter along with IV antibiotics and admission.

questions.text: Which of the following clinical situations requires urgent decompression of the urinary tract?
options: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
originalOptions: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
questions.correctAnswer: C) An obstructed, infected collecting system
questions.explanation: An obstructed and infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urologic emergency requiring urgent decompression via JJ stent or nephrostomy to prevent sepsis and renal destruction.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of long-term double-J (JJ) ureteral stenting?
questions.explanation: Long-standing catheters (not JJ stents specifically) are linked to stone formation and bladder cancer risk with prolonged indwelling urethral catheters; urothelial cancer is not a typical direct complication attributed to JJ stents, whose common complications are infection, hematuria, and irritative/positional flank pain.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medications used for overactive bladder?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, and confusion, due to inhibition of parasympathetic (muscarinic) activity on the gut and other organs.

questions.text: A fetus is found to have antenatal hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound. Appropriate postnatal evaluation includes:
options: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
originalOptions: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswer: A) Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.explanation: Postnatal workup of antenatal hydronephrosis is guided by severity, using renal ultrasound as the initial test, followed by VCUG (to assess for reflux) and/or renal scan (to assess function/obstruction) as indicated.

questions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have mild hydronephrosis on ultrasound with no symptoms of infection or stone disease. This is most likely explained by:
options: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
originalOptions: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswerText: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.explanation: Mild hydronephrosis in pregnancy, particularly on the right side, is commonly physiological due to compression of the ureter by the enlarging gravid uterus and does not necessarily indicate pathology.

questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ER after a motorcycle accident with a deceleration mechanism. He has flank ecchymosis and gross hematuria. What is the single best indicator of significant renal injury in this patient?
questions.explanation: Hematuria is the best indicator of significant renal injury, though its degree does not correlate reliably with injury severity, so imaging decisions are not based on hematuria grade alone.

questions.text: A 40-year-old man sustains a stab wound to the flank. Compared to blunt renal trauma, penetrating renal trauma is characterized by:
options: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
Lower likelihood of requiring surgical intervention
originalOptions: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
Lower likelihood of requiring surgical intervention
questions.correctAnswer: B) Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
questions.correctAnswerText: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
questions.explanation: Penetrating trauma (gunshot/stab) causes a higher rate of complications and more often requires surgical intervention than blunt trauma.

questions.text: Which finding is most specifically associated with reno-vascular (pedicle) injury after blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: Significant deceleration causes tearing at points of fixation such as the renal hilum, making this the key historical clue for vascular injury.

questions.text: A hemodynamically stable adult sustains blunt abdominal trauma with one documented episode of hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) and microscopic hematuria. Renal imaging is indicated because:
options: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
All blunt trauma requires imaging regardless of findings
Imaging is never needed if hematuria is microscopic
Imaging is reserved for penetrating trauma only
originalOptions: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
All blunt trauma requires imaging regardless of findings
Imaging is never needed if hematuria is microscopic
Imaging is reserved for penetrating trauma only
questions.correctAnswer: A) Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
questions.correctAnswerText: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma with microscopic hematuria plus even one episode of hypotension (SBP <90) is a specific indication for renal imaging, unlike simple stable microscopic hematuria.

questions.text: The gold standard imaging modality for suspected renal trauma is:
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for renal trauma, allowing grading of injury and assessment of associated structures (hilum, perinephric space, vena cava).

questions.text: One-shot intraoperative IVP performed during renal trauma surgery is primarily used to:
options: Grade the degree of renal laceration
Assess function of the contralateral kidney
originalOptions: Grade the degree of renal laceration
Assess function of the contralateral kidney
questions.correctAnswer: C) Assess function of the contralateral kidney
questions.correctAnswerText: Assess function of the contralateral kidney
questions.explanation: The one-shot IVP (10 minutes after IV contrast push) is mainly used intraoperatively to confirm that the contralateral kidney is functioning before proceeding with nephrectomy if needed.

questions.text: Which of the following is the primary criterion guiding management of renal trauma?
options: Presence of gross vs microscopic hematuria
originalOptions: Presence of gross vs microscopic hematuria
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic stability is the primary criterion determining management; stable patients are typically managed conservatively regardless of imaging grade, unstable patients require intervention.

questions.text: Selective angio-embolization is most indicated in renal trauma when CT shows:
options: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
originalOptions: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
questions.correctAnswer: A) Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
questions.correctAnswerText: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
questions.explanation: CT findings of active contrast extravasation, arteriovenous fistula, or aneurysm are indications for selective angio-embolization.

questions.text: Which of the following is an indication for renal exploration after trauma?
options: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
Stable patient with contrast leak amenable to embolization
originalOptions: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
Stable patient with contrast leak amenable to embolization
questions.correctAnswer: C) Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
questions.explanation: An expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma discovered at laparotomy, along with non-response to resuscitation, grade 5 vascular injury, or failed embolization, are indications for surgical exploration.

questions.text: A patient with pelvic fracture and gross hematuria is suspected of having a bladder injury. Which imaging study should be performed to exclude bladder rupture?
questions.explanation: Any patient with pelvic fracture and gross (visible) hematuria should undergo cystography to exclude bladder rupture, as visible hematuria is the principal sign of bladder trauma.

questions.text: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture most commonly results from:
options: A sudden blow to a distended bladder
Spontaneous rupture in a healthy bladder
originalOptions: A sudden blow to a distended bladder
Spontaneous rupture in a healthy bladder
questions.explanation: Extraperitoneal bladder injury is almost always secondary to pelvic fracture, whereas intraperitoneal rupture typically results from a blow to a distended bladder raising intravesical pressure.

questions.text: On cystography, intraperitoneal bladder rupture is classically identified by:
options: Flame-shaped extravasation in perivesical soft tissue
Contrast pooling only within the bladder lumen
Extravasation limited to the prostatic urethra
originalOptions: Flame-shaped extravasation in perivesical soft tissue
Contrast pooling only within the bladder lumen
Extravasation limited to the prostatic urethra
questions.correctAnswer: A) Contrast leak outlining bowel loops
questions.explanation: Intraperitoneal rupture shows contrast outlining bowel loops as it leaks into the peritoneal cavity, while extraperitoneal rupture shows a flame-shaped perivesical extravasation pattern.

questions.text: Management of an isolated extraperitoneal bladder rupture without bladder neck involvement is:
options: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
originalOptions: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
questions.correctAnswer: C) Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
questions.correctAnswerText: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture is managed conservatively with Foley catheter drainage; surgery is reserved for bladder neck involvement or associated injuries. Intraperitoneal rupture, in contrast, always requires surgical repair.

questions.text: A man reports a popping sound during vigorous intercourse followed by immediate detumescence, pain, and eggplant-shaped swelling of the penis. Blood is noted at the urethral meatus. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Immediate surgical exploration without further workup
Blind Foley catheter placement to relieve retention
originalOptions: Immediate surgical exploration without further workup
Blind Foley catheter placement to relieve retention
questions.explanation: Blood at the urethral meatus after suspected penile fracture indicates possible urethral injury; a retrograde urethrogram must be performed before attempting catheterization.

questions.text: In penile fracture, the structure that must be surgically repaired is the:
questions.explanation: Penile fracture is a tear of the tunica albuginea; surgical exploration, hematoma evacuation, and closure of this tear is the definitive management and reduces complications compared with conservative treatment.

allQuestions.text: BPH most commonly arises from which zone of the prostate?
allQuestions.explanation: BPH develops in the transitional zone, whereas prostate cancer arises predominantly (70–80%) from the peripheral zone.

allQuestions.text: In uncomplicated bladder outflow obstruction due to BPH, which finding is typical?
options: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
originalOptions: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
allQuestions.explanation: A maximum flow rate below 15 mL/sec (with <10 mL/sec strongly suggestive) is typical of obstruction. Finasteride takes 6+ months to work, and alpha-blockers (not agonists) relieve symptoms.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT assessed by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)?
allQuestions.explanation: IPSS assesses seven voiding/storage symptoms (incomplete emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, nocturia) but does not include incontinence, As a key word (FUN II SS) frequency,urgency,nocturnal , incomplete empathy,intermittent,stream is weak ,straining

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of the voiding (obstructive) phase in BPH?
allQuestions.explanation: Frequency is a storage symptom. Voiding/obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, weak stream, straining, intermittency, and terminal dribbling.

allQuestions.text: Which symptom is NOT related to urine storage phase dysfunction?
allQuestions.explanation: Weak stream is a voiding (obstructive) phase symptom. Storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has an IPSS of 22 (severe). What is the best initial treatment?
allQuestions.explanation: Alpha-1 blockers such as terazosin are first-line medical therapy for BPH, even with severe IPSS scores. Surgery is reserved for failed medical therapy or complications.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT used in the treatment of BPH?
allQuestions.explanation: Alpha-1 agonists cause smooth muscle contraction and would worsen bladder outflow obstruction. Beta-blockers also have no established role in BPH, but alpha-agonists are the classically incorrect option since they directly oppose the mechanism of alpha-blocker therapy.

allQuestions.text: Tamsulosin, used in the treatment of BPH, acts as a(n):
allQuestions.explanation: Tamsulosin is a selective alpha-1A antagonist that relaxes prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle to improve urinary flow.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an indication for open (simple) prostatectomy rather than TURP?
options: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
originalOptions: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Prostate size greater than 80 grams
allQuestions.explanation: A prostate weighing more than 80 g is generally too large for safe transurethral resection (increased TUR syndrome risk), making open (or laparoscopic/robotic) simple prostatectomy preferable.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about anticholinergic drugs in BPH is FALSE?
options: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
originalOptions: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics are contraindicated, not indicated, when PVR exceeds 150 mL, due to the risk of precipitating acute urinary retention.

allQuestions.text: Antimuscarinic therapy for LUTS/BPH is contraindicated:
options: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
originalOptions: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
allQuestions.explanation: Antimuscarinics are contraindicated specifically in men with large, persistent PVR due to retention risk; they can safely be combined with alpha-blockers for mixed storage and voiding symptoms.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic medications?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation (not diarrhea), along with dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized side effect of tamsulosin?
allQuestions.explanation: Tamsulosin's known side effects are retrograde ejaculation (most common), postural hypotension, and rhinitis/nasal congestion; decreased libido is not a typical alpha-blocker side effect.

allQuestions.text: Regarding post-void residual (PVR) assessment in BPH, which statement is most accurate?
options: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
originalOptions: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
allQuestions.explanation: PVR is typically measured using ultrasound (avoiding invasive catheterization) and should be assessed in patients with significant voiding symptoms or before certain interventions, though it is not measured after every single void.

allQuestions.text: Which symptom is LEAST specific for bladder outflow obstruction?
allQuestions.explanation: Nocturia can result from many causes (polyuria, cardiac disease, aging) besides bladder outflow obstruction, making it the least specific symptom among the choices.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a storage symptom of BPH?
allQuestions.explanation: Dysuria reflects pain during urination (typically from inflammation) and is not a standard storage LUTS; storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following does NOT occur during the voiding phase?
allQuestions.explanation: Nocturia is a storage-phase symptom, while hesitancy and weak stream are voiding-phase symptoms.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old man with LUTS has IPSS 22 and PVR 50 mL. The most appropriate next step is:
allQuestions.explanation: With a severe IPSS but only mildly elevated PVR and no indication for surgery, first-line medical therapy with an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) is appropriate.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has IPSS symptom score of 22, PVR 50 cc, prostate volume 60 cc, severe detrusor instability on cystometrogram, and high-grade obstruction on pressure-flow study. The best next step to improve symptoms is:
allQuestions.explanation: Despite urodynamic evidence of obstruction and detrusor overactivity, initial management remains medical therapy with an alpha-blocker before considering surgery, given no absolute surgical indication is present.

allQuestions.text: A 65-year-old man on tamsulosin and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for 2 months continues to have obstructive symptoms. The next step is:
options: Continue current therapy and reassess later
originalOptions: Continue current therapy and reassess later
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Continue current therapy and reassess later
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Continue current therapy and reassess later
allQuestions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors require at least 6 months to show clinical benefit; persistent symptoms after only 3 months, without complications, warrant continued therapy and reassessment rather than surgery.

allQuestions.text: Tamsulosin combined with a PDE5 inhibitor should be used with caution due to the risk of:
allQuestions.explanation: Both alpha-blockers and PDE5 inhibitors cause vasodilation; their combination increases the risk of significant hypotension.

allQuestions.text: Which bladder tumor originates from the urachus?
allQuestions.explanation: Urachal remnants at the bladder dome give rise to adenocarcinoma, often presenting with mucusuria. TCC and SCC arise from urothelium and chronic irritation respectively, not urachal remnants.

allQuestions.text: Which type of bladder cancer is caused due to chronic irritation?
allQuestions.explanation: Chronic irritation (Schistosoma, long-term catheterization, bladder stones, recurrent UTI) causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, progressing to SCC over time.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following environmental factors is highly associated with bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Smoking accounts for roughly half of bladder cancers, conferring a 2–6× increased risk via carcinogenic arylamines. Occupational and radiation exposure are recognized risk factors but contribute far less overall.

allQuestions.text: Typical presentation of bladder cancer:
allQuestions.explanation: This is the classic presentation, seen in 80–85% of patients, and represents total hematuria from the bladder. Irritative symptoms like frequency or dysuria are less common and suggest CIS.

allQuestions.text: 68-year-old male patient diagnosed with bladder TCC; on TURBT histology came back as T2 bladder TCC. Best next treatment option is:i
allQuestions.explanation: T2 disease invades the muscularis propria, defining muscle-invasive bladder cancer, which requires radical cystectomy (± neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy). Intravesical therapies are reserved for non-muscle-invasive disease.

allQuestions.text: Which is considered the best for follow-up of bladder cancer after resection?
allQuestions.explanation: Cystoscopy is the gold standard for surveillance, allowing direct visualization and biopsy of recurrent lesions. Imaging modalities lack the sensitivity to detect small mucosal recurrences.

allQuestions.text: Which one of the following intravesical treatments CANNOT be given immediately after bladder cancer resection?
allQuestions.explanation: Intravesical chemotherapy (such as Mitomycin) can be administered as a single dose within 24 hours of resection to eliminate circulating tumor cells. However, intravesical BCG (an attenuated strain of mycobacteria) must be delayed for at least 2 weeks post-resection. This delay allows the resection site to heal completely, preventing potentially fatal systemic mycobacterial dissemination and BCG-sepsis.

allQuestions.text: High-grade bladder tumor characteristics:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) High progression AND high recurrence
allQuestions.explanation: High-grade tumors carry both high recurrence and high progression risk, whereas low-grade tumors have high recurrence but low progression potential.

allQuestions.text: A 62-year-old male presents with intermittent, painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a papillary bladder tumor, and he undergoes a complete transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). The final histopathology report confirms a Ta, low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the immediate management of this patient?
allQuestions.explanation: A single immediate instillation post-TURBT reduces recurrence by ~50% in Ta low-grade tumors. BCG is reserved for T1, CIS, or high-grade Ta disease due to its higher toxicity.

allQuestions.text: Egyptian man with previous Schistosoma parasite infection — most common bladder cancer type:
allQuestions.explanation: S. haematobium is endemic in Egypt; eggs deposited in the bladder wall trigger chronic inflammation and squamous metaplasia, leading to SCC rather than TCC.

allQuestions.text: Risk factor for bladder cancer from occupation:
allQuestions.explanation: Aromatic amines such as benzidine and beta-naphthylamine are established occupational carcinogens in these industries, as well as in painting and hairdressing.

allQuestions.text: What is the definitive treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion is the gold standard for T2+ disease. Chemotherapy alone and intravesical therapy are inadequate once muscularis propria is invaded.

allQuestions.text: Which group is more affected by bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Male:female ratio is roughly 3:1, with peak incidence at 60–70 years; smoking further amplifies this predominant demographic risk.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a risk factor for bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines in the rubber industry is a well-established, strong risk factor. Family history confers only a modest (two-fold) increase in comparison.

allQuestions.text: Patient with uncontrolled HTN, colon cancer treated with cyclophosphamide + radiotherapy, now has invasive bladder cancer — what is LEAST likely to increase bladder cancer risk?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypertension is not a recognized bladder cancer risk factor, whereas cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiotherapy, and smoking are all established causative agents.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a common risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder?
allQuestions.explanation: Eggs lodging in the bladder wall provoke chronic granulomatous inflammation and squamous metaplasia, culminating in SCC — unlike ordinary bacterial UTIs.

allQuestions.text: 60-year-old smoker with painless intermittent gross hematuria. Most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) TCC (transitional cell carcinoma) bladder cancer
allQuestions.explanation: TCC accounts for ~90% of bladder cancers and is strongly linked to smoking, presenting classically with painless intermittent gross hematuria.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Alcohol has no established causal link to bladder cancer, unlike smoking, occupational carcinogen exposure, and male gender, which are all recognized risk factors.

allQuestions.text: Most common cancer associated with persistent urachus:
allQuestions.explanation: A persistent urachal remnant at the bladder dome predisposes to adenocarcinoma, distinct from the urothelium-derived TCC affecting the rest of the bladder.

allQuestions.text: Patient with bladder cancer stage T1, high risk for progression, underwent resection; after 2 weeks what is the next step?
allQuestions.explanation: High-risk T1 tumors require re-resection (repeat TURBT) to exclude understaging or residual disease before committing to intravesical therapy.

allQuestions.text: Patient treated with BCG has a biopsy showing CIS with muscle invasion. What is the best management?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion
allQuestions.explanation: Muscle invasion signifies progression beyond the scope of intravesical therapy; BCG failure with invasive disease mandates radical cystectomy.

allQuestions.text: Patient found to have bladder cancer; after TURBT the histology came back as T1. What is the next step?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Cystoscopy follow-up and intravesical therapy
allQuestions.explanation: T1 tumors are non-muscle-invasive, so management consists of surveillance cystoscopy with intravesical instillation rather than radical surgery.

allQuestions.text: The most common presentation of bladder cancer:
allQuestions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria is the classic and most common presenting symptom, seen in the majority of bladder cancer patients.

allQuestions.text: Urine cytology is most sensitive for?
options: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
originalOptions: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
allQuestions.explanation: Urine cytology detects poorly differentiated cells shed from high-grade tumors and CIS with high sensitivity, but often misses well-differentiated low-grade lesions.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a component of trimodal therapy for bladder-preserving treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Trimodal therapy combines maximal TURBT with concurrent chemotherapy and radiotherapy specifically to spare the bladder; radical cystectomy is the alternative it aims to avoid.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes the classical presentation of bladder cancer, particularly when carcinoma in situ is present?
options: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
originalOptions: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
allQuestions.explanation: Classic presentation is painless intermittent hematuria; irritative symptoms suggest CIS.

allQuestions.text: Which chemotherapeutic agent is itself a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: Its urotoxic metabolite (acrolein) damages the urothelium, increasing bladder cancer risk.

allQuestions.text: A low-risk non-muscle-invasive tumor is resected. Most appropriate immediate management?
allQuestions.explanation: A single post-TURBT instillation reduces recurrence in low-risk disease without BCG-level toxicity.

allQuestions.text: A high-risk T1, high-grade tumor is found after TURBT. Recommended intravesical therapy?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Induction BCG followed by maintenance
allQuestions.explanation: High-risk T1/high-grade or CIS requires induction BCG plus maintenance for optimal recurrence/progression control.

allQuestions.text: Which finding after TURBT mandates repeat TURBT?
options: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
originalOptions: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
allQuestions.explanation: These carry understaging risk, so repeat TURBT confirms true depth of invasion before further treatment.

allQuestions.text: A patient has very-high-risk or BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. Best management?
allQuestions.explanation: BCG-unresponsive or very-high-risk disease carries high progression risk, favoring cystectomy over further intravesical salvage.

allQuestions.text: Which correctly differentiates timing of chemotherapy vs. BCG after TURBT?
options: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
BCG within 24 hours; chemotherapy delayed 2 weeks
originalOptions: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
BCG within 24 hours; chemotherapy delayed 2 weeks
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
allQuestions.explanation: Immediate chemo reduces recurrence; BCG needs intact urothelium to avoid systemic dissemination.

allQuestions.text: An IVU during the bladder-filling phase shows a radiolucent filling defect. Most likely diagnosis? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: A radiolucent filling defect on IVU most commonly represents a urothelial tumor projecting into the lumen.

allQuestions.text: Given a radiolucent bladder filling defect on IVU, which is LEAST likely as a differential? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Pyelonephritis is a renal parenchymal infection and does not cause a bladder filling defect.

allQuestions.text: A radiolucent bladder filling defect is seen with hematuria. Next step? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
options: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
originalOptions: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Cystoscopy with TURBT for diagnosis and staging
allQuestions.explanation: TURBT gives histological diagnosis and staging; cytology/imaging are adjuncts, not substitutes.

allQuestions.text: This imaging study was performed during the bladder-filling phase, showing a radiolucent filling defect. What is the name of this imaging study? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: IVU uses IV contrast excreted by the kidneys to opacify the collecting system, ureters, and bladder, allowing detection of filling defects such as tumors.

allQuestions.text: Regarding urological imaging studies, what is the most important risk of exposure to ionizing radiation?
allQuestions.explanation: Ionizing radiation from CT and fluoroscopic urological studies carries a cumulative risk of carcinogenesis, making malignancy induction the most clinically significant long-term hazard. options: Kidneys lie posterior in the abdomen

allQuestions.explanation: Kidneys lie retroperitoneally against the posterior abdominal wall, not within the peritoneal cavity. All other listed features (bilateral, bean-shaped, posterior location) accurately describe renal anatomy.

allQuestions.text: The correct order of the division of the intrarenal branches of the renal artery is:
allQuestions.explanation: The renal artery branches sequentially from segmental arteries into interlobar arteries running between pyramids, then arcuate arteries arching at the corticomedullary junction, and finally interlobular arteries ascending into the cortex.

allQuestions.text: The only segment of the urethra that does NOT have transitional epithelium is the:
allQuestions.explanation: The fossa navicularis is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, distinguishing it from the transitional epithelium lining the more proximal urethral segments listed as options. Another way to phrase the question: Which segment is lined by stratified squamous epithelium? Ans: E.

allQuestions.text: Ultrasound has many advantages which include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: It is safe and does not use ionizing radiation

It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
It can be safely performed in pregnant women

It can be safely performed in pregnant women

allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It allows discrimination between pseudotumors and true lesions
allQuestions.explanation: Ultrasound is limited in differentiating pseudotumors from true renal lesions; CT or MRI are superior for this characterization. Its safety, minimal preparation, and independence from renal function are genuine advantages.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is associated with suprapubic pain?
allQuestions.explanation: Bladder pathology such as cystitis or overdistension classically produces suprapubic discomfort, whereas renal colic and ureteric stones typically cause flank pain radiating to the groin.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding physical examination?
options: The testes in men should be the same size
The normal prostate is the size of a walnut
A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
It is best to examine a man's genitalia in a warm room

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: A hydrocele feels like a bag of worms
allQuestions.explanation: A "bag of worms" texture describes a varicocele, not a hydrocele; a hydrocele is a smooth, fluid-filled swelling that transilluminates. A warm room helps relax the cremasteric reflex for accurate examination.

allQuestions.text: All the following can cause a DECREASE in specific gravity of urine EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Dehydration concentrates the urine, raising specific gravity, whereas increased fluid intake, diuretics, and impaired concentrating ability all dilute urine and lower specific gravity.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following are used in the calculation of plasma osmolarity?
allQuestions.explanation: Plasma osmolarity is estimated as 2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, incorporating sodium as the main osmotic contributor along with glucose and urea.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is true about renal pain?
options: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
originalOptions: Caused by acute distension of renal capsule from obstruction or inflammation
Can be confused with intraperitoneal diseases
allQuestions.explanation: Renal pain arises from capsular distension, with inflammatory pain being steady while obstructive pain fluctuates; it can also mimic intraperitoneal pathology, though patients with renal pain classically prefer to move (rolling sign) unlike those with peritoneal pain.

allQuestions.text: Choose the WRONG statement about kidney anatomy:
options: Right kidney is 1 cm higher than the left kidney
Left kidney is higher than the right
Right kidney extends from 1st to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
Left kidney extends from 12th thoracic to 3rd lumbar vertebrae
The right kidney is displaced inferiorly by the liver

allQuestions.text: Choose the WRONG statement:

allQuestions.explanation: This reverses the actual pattern: inflammatory renal pain is steady, while obstructive pain fluctuates in intensity as the ureter undergoes hyperperistalsis to overcome the blockage.

allQuestions.text: Radiographically, the ureter is divided into how many parts?
allQuestions.explanation: The ureter is anatomically and radiologically divided into upper, middle (over the sacrum), and lower segments, corresponding to abdominal, pelvic, and intramural portions.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following drugs does NOT cause renal failure?
allQuestions.explanation: Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used for bladder outlet obstruction and lacks nephrotoxic potential, unlike ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, and NSAIDs, which can impair renal perfusion or cause direct tubular injury.

allQuestions.text: Which imaging modality is safest for a patient in renal failure?
allQuestions.explanation: Ultrasound requires no contrast or radiation exposure and is unaffected by renal function, making it the safest imaging choice in renal impairment, unlike iodinated or gadolinium-based contrast studies which risk nephrotoxicity or nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

allQuestions.text: Renal pain classically radiates to which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain radiates from the flank toward the groin and may be referred to the testis due to shared T11-T12 innervation, distinguishing it from intraperitoneal pain, which classically radiates to the shoulder.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the male urethra from proximal to distal?
allQuestions.explanation: The male urethra begins at the bladder neck, passing through the prostatic segment, then the membranous urethra at the external sphincter, followed by the bulbar and pendulous penile urethra ending at the fossa navicularis.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with flank pain. Which feature would favor a urological (renal) rather than an intraperitoneal cause?
options: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs

Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
allQuestions.explanation: Renal colic patients characteristically move restlessly (rolling sign) due to colicky pain, whereas intraperitoneal pathology causes steady pain with patients preferring to remain motionless.

allQuestions.text: Pneumaturia is best defined as which of the following?
options: Presence of gas in the urine
Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine
originalOptions: Presence of gas in the urine
Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Presence of gas in the urine
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Presence of gas in the urine
allQuestions.explanation: Pneumaturia results from recent catheterization, an enteric fistula, or infection with gas-forming organisms, distinguishing it from hematuria (blood) or enuresis (nocturnal incontinence).

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a FALSE statement about gonadal veins?
options: The right gonadal vein terminates in the inferior vena cava below the level of the right renal vein
The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava

allQuestions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation presents with new-onset gross hematuria and mild flank discomfort, with no fever or dysuria. What is the best initial investigation?
allQuestions.explanation: Ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation and contrast, making it the safest first-line imaging choice in pregnancy for evaluating hematuria.
