allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Essential investigations: cystoscopy and upper tract imaging; Causes: urinary tract stones, urothelial/renal malignancy, glomerular disease
allQuestions.explanation: Hematuria in an adult is malignancy until proven otherwise, so cystoscopy assesses the bladder while upper tract imaging evaluates the kidneys and ureters, with stones, malignancy, and glomerular disease as the key causes to exclude. The distractors instead describe irritative symptom workup, scrotal pathology, or bladder outlet obstruction assessment, none of which target hematuria evaluation.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are appropriate questions to ask when taking a history of hematuria EXCEPT:
options: Is the blood present at the start, throughout, or at the end of the urinary stream?
Is the hematuria associated with pain, or is it painless?
Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
originalOptions: Is the blood present at the start, throughout, or at the end of the urinary stream?
Is the hematuria associated with pain, or is it painless?
Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
allQuestions.explanation: Timing of blood in the stream, presence or absence of pain, clot characteristics, and smoking or occupational exposure history are all directly relevant to localizing and risk-stratifying hematuria, whereas morning stiffness is a rheumatological question unrelated to urological assessment.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are irritative LUTS symptoms EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Hesitancy is an obstructive symptom reflecting delayed initiation of urination, whereas frequency, urgency, nocturia, and dysuria are all irritative symptoms related to bladder storage and mucosal irritation.

allQuestions.text: A 68-year-old man reports voiding 10 times during the day and waking up 3 times at night to urinate, each time passing only a small volume, with a strong sudden desire to void that is difficult to defer. His total 24-hour urine output is normal. Which category of symptoms best describes this presentation?
allQuestions.explanation: Frequency, nocturia with small voided volumes, and urgency despite a normal total daily urine output point to decreased functional bladder capacity or mucosal irritation, characteristic of irritative rather than obstructive symptoms.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes true hematuria from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria?
allQuestions.explanation: Dipstick is positive for blood in all three conditions, but only true hematuria shows intact red blood cells on microscopic urinalysis.

allQuestions.text: A patient reports blood appearing only at the very end of the urinary stream, after most of the urine has already passed. This pattern of terminal hematuria most suggests pathology arising from:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Bladder neck or prostatic inflammation
allQuestions.explanation: Initial hematuria localizes to the urethra, total hematuria to the bladder or upper tract, and terminal hematuria to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra.

allQuestions.text: A 68-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless gross hematuria. Which diagnosis must be excluded first as the classic cause of painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 years old?
allQuestions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, warranting cystoscopy and upper tract imaging regardless of other findings.

allQuestions.text: A normotensive patient is found to have isolated microscopic hematuria on routine urinalysis, with no other urinary symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate initial action?
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria in a low-risk patient is initially managed conservatively with a repeat urinalysis rather than immediate invasive workup.

allQuestions.text: When taking a history from a patient presenting with hematuria, which combination of questions is most important to ask?
allQuestions.explanation: Onset, presence of clots, and timing during the urinary stream all help localize the source and severity of hematuria, so all should be asked.

allQuestions.text: Hematuria in an adult should be treated as a warning sign of which of the following until proven otherwise?
allQuestions.explanation: Although hematuria has many causes, it is classically taught that hematuria in an adult signals malignancy, most often bladder cancer, until excluded.

allQuestions.text: A 70-year-old male smoker presents with gross hematuria persisting for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
allQuestions.explanation: Persistent gross hematuria in an older smoker requires full evaluation of both the upper tract (CT urogram) and lower tract (cystoscopy) to exclude urothelial malignancy.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about carcinoma of the prostate is correct?
options: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
originalOptions: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
allQuestions.explanation: Prostate cancer is an adenocarcinoma graded by the Gleason score, arises predominantly in the peripheral zone, is hormone-dependent (responds to androgen deprivation therapy), and rarely invades the rectum due to Denonvilliers' fascia.

allQuestions.text: What grading system is used for prostate cancer?
allQuestions.explanation: The Gleason score assesses glandular architecture on low-power microscopy and correlates with prognosis; Bloom-Richardson is used for breast cancer, Breslow for melanoma, and Fuhrman for renal cell carcinoma.

allQuestions.text: PSA density is calculated as:
options: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
originalOptions: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
allQuestions.explanation: PSA density is total serum PSA divided by prostate volume (measured by TRUS); values above 0.15 ng/mL/g raise suspicion for malignancy.

allQuestions.text: Serum PSA and digital rectal examination are primarily used for:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Early detection/screening for prostate cancer
allQuestions.explanation: PSA testing combined with DRE is used for early detection of prostate cancer in asymptomatic men, though PSA is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific.

allQuestions.text: Watchful waiting (as opposed to active surveillance) is most appropriate for men who:
options: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
originalOptions: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
allQuestions.explanation: Watchful waiting is a palliative, symptom-directed strategy reserved for patients with limited life expectancy (≤10 years) and less aggressive disease, distinct from active surveillance which is used in younger, low-risk patients with curative intent.

allQuestions.text: The most common site of prostate cancer metastasis is:
allQuestions.explanation: Prostate cancer classically metastasizes to the axial skeleton, particularly the lumbar spine, producing osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions with associated back pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

allQuestions.text: Which statement about the Gleason grading system is FALSE?
options: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
originalOptions: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) It does not correlate with prognosis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It does not correlate with prognosis
allQuestions.explanation: This statement is false — the Gleason score strongly correlates with prognosis and guides management decisions in prostate cancer.

allQuestions.text: Serum PSA elevation may occur in association with which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: PSA is organ-specific, not disease-specific, and can be elevated by BPH, prostatitis, cancer, and mechanical manipulation of the prostate (e.g., catheterization, biopsy, DRE).

allQuestions.text: Which is the most common cancer diagnosed in urology?
allQuestions.explanation: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer diagnosed in men overall and the most common urological malignancy.

allQuestions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has a Gleason score of 8 and PSA 25. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate management option?
allQuestions.explanation: Active surveillance is reserved for low-risk disease; a Gleason score of 8 with PSA 25 indicates high-risk disease requiring definitive treatment such as surgery or radiotherapy with hormonal therapy.

allQuestions.text: A patient with Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer is best managed with:
allQuestions.explanation: Gleason 3+3 (grade group 1) represents low-risk disease, for which active surveillance is generally preferred to avoid overtreatment, provided other risk factors (PSA, stage, patient preference) support this approach.

allQuestions.text: A patient has a suspicious prostatic mass on digital rectal exam with PSA of 9 ng/mL. The next step is:
allQuestions.explanation: A suspicious DRE finding combined with elevated PSA warrants histological diagnosis via ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy rather than proceeding directly to surveillance or watchful waiting.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are indications for prostate biopsy EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: A high free:total PSA ratio (such as 30%) is reassuring and associated with a lower likelihood of cancer; a low ratio would instead raise suspicion and support biopsy.

allQuestions.text: The Gleason score is used specifically for grading:
allQuestions.explanation: The Gleason score is a histological grading system exclusively for prostate adenocarcinoma, based on glandular differentiation patterns.

allQuestions.text: A patient with known advanced prostate cancer presents with new-onset back pain. The most appropriate immediate step is:
options: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
originalOptions: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
allQuestions.explanation: New back pain in a patient with known prostate cancer must first be evaluated for vertebral metastasis or spinal cord compression as an oncologic emergency; systemic androgen-deprivation therapy (GnRH/LHRH agonist) is appropriate for the underlying metastatic disease once red flags are excluded.

allQuestions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has Gleason grade 8 and PSA greater than 20 with no metastatic findings on staging. Which management option is NOT appropriate?
allQuestions.explanation: Active surveillance is unsuitable for high-risk, non-metastatic disease (Gleason 8, PSA >20); definitive treatment with surgery or radiotherapy plus hormonal therapy is indicated.

allQuestions.text: After one year of therapy with a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, PSA typically:
allQuestions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors reduce PSA levels by approximately 50% after 6–12 months of therapy; this must be accounted for when interpreting PSA values in patients on these drugs.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common presentation of renal cell carcinoma?
options: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
originalOptions: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
allQuestions.explanation: Most RCCs are now discovered incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons; the classic triad occurs in fewer than 10% of cases.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common histopathological subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
allQuestions.explanation: Clear cell RCC accounts for approximately 75% of RCC cases, is associated with VHL gene mutations, and carries the worst prognosis among the common subtypes.

allQuestions.text: The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with RCC is:
allQuestions.explanation: Hypercalcemia, mediated via PTHrP secretion, is the most common paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC.

allQuestions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with 2 months of painless visible hematuria, hypertension, weight loss, low-grade fever, and anemia. The most likely diagnosis is:
allQuestions.explanation: Painless visible hematuria with hypertension and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fever, anemia) reflects the paraneoplastic and systemic presentation classically associated with renal cell carcinoma.

allQuestions.text: Renal cell carcinoma is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: A vegetarian diet is not an established risk factor for RCC; recognized risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, long-term dialysis (ESRD), and inherited syndromes such as VHL disease.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with pneumothorax, cutaneous fibrofolliculomas, and a renal tumor. The most likely RCC subtype is:
allQuestions.explanation: This triad is characteristic of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, which is associated with chromophobe/oncocytic renal tumors, skin fibrofolliculomas, and pulmonary cysts predisposing to pneumothorax.

allQuestions.text: A patient has an RCC measuring 4 cm confined to the kidney. The preferred treatment is:
allQuestions.explanation: Partial nephrectomy is preferred for T1 tumors (≤7 cm) when technically feasible, as it provides equivalent oncologic outcomes to radical nephrectomy while preserving renal function.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC?
allQuestions.explanation: Increased serotonin is not a recognized paraneoplastic feature of RCC; recognized paraneoplastic syndromes include erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and Stauffer's syndrome (hepatic dysfunction without metastases).

allQuestions.text: The classic triad of renal cell carcinoma consists of:
options: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
originalOptions: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
allQuestions.explanation: The classic (but now uncommon) triad of RCC is hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable flank mass, occurring together in less than 10% of patients.

allQuestions.text: The most common site of RCC metastasis is:
allQuestions.explanation: The lung is the most common site of metastasis for renal cell carcinoma, followed by bone and liver.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an established risk factor for renal cell carcinoma?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypertension is a well-established risk factor for RCC, along with smoking, obesity, and long-term dialysis; alcohol and diabetes are not classically listed among the primary risk factors.

allQuestions.text: Most cases of renal cell carcinoma are discovered:
allQuestions.explanation: The majority of RCCs are detected incidentally during imaging performed for unrelated indications, reflecting the often silent early course of the disease.

allQuestions.text: A patient with RCC presents with elevated hemoglobin (erythrocytosis). Which hormone is responsible?
allQuestions.explanation: Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by the tumor causes paraneoplastic erythrocytosis in RCC; PTHrP causes hypercalcemia, not erythrocytosis.

allQuestions.text: A 42-year-old Black male with known sickle cell disease is diagnosed with RCC. The most likely subtype is:
allQuestions.explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait/disease and typically occurs in young Black patients, distinguishing it from the other subtypes.

allQuestions.text: A patient is found to have a solid 4x5 cm renal mass in the lower pole. The next step in evaluation is:
allQuestions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for characterizing a solid renal mass, as it allows assessment of enhancement (the key feature distinguishing RCC from benign lesions) and staging.

allQuestions.text: A key imaging characteristic of tumors associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is:
allQuestions.explanation: VHL-associated clear cell RCC tumors are characteristically hypervascular due to upregulation of angiogenic factors from loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following are established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma?
options: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
originalOptions: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
allQuestions.explanation: ESRD, Smoking, obesity, and hypertension are all recognized, established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized paraneoplastic syndrome in RCC?
allQuestions.explanation: Polycythemia (erythrocytosis) due to ectopic erythropoietin secretion is a well-recognized paraneoplastic syndrome of RCC; RCC is in fact the most common cause of paraneoplastic erythrocytosis

allQuestions.text: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, nausea, bradycardia, and hypertension near the end of a prolonged resection. Serum sodium is low. This is best explained by:
options: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
originalOptions: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
allQuestions.explanation: TUR syndrome results from absorption of hypotonic irrigating solution through open venous sinuses during resection, causing hypervolemic hyponatremia with confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and visual disturbances.

allQuestions.text: Which factor is most associated with increased risk of TUR syndrome?
options: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
originalOptions: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Resection time greater than 90 minutes
allQuestions.explanation: TUR syndrome risk increases with resection times exceeding 90 minutes and is more common in older men; bipolar TURP performed under saline (isotonic) irrigation reduces this risk.

allQuestions.text: A patient requires long-term indwelling catheterization. Compared to latex, silicone catheters are preferred because they:
options: Are only available in smaller sizes
originalOptions: Are only available in smaller sizes
allQuestions.explanation: Silicone catheters induce less tissue inflammation than latex, making them preferable for long-term catheterization, despite latex being cheaper and more widely available.

allQuestions.text: A 24 French Foley catheter has an outer diameter of approximately:
allQuestions.explanation: Catheter French size divided by 3 gives the outer diameter in millimeters; 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized indication for urethral catheterization?
options: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
originalOptions: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
allQuestions.explanation: Monitoring urine output is a standard, common indication for catheterization. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, pelvic fracture with urethral disruption) is a contraindication until imaging excludes injury.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to transurethral Foley catheter placement?
options: Need for a clean urine sample
originalOptions: Need for a clean urine sample
allQuestions.explanation: Suspected urethral injury is a contraindication to urethral catheterization; a retrograde urethrogram should be performed first, and a suprapubic catheter used if drainage is needed.

allQuestions.text: Chronic urinary retention is best distinguished from acute retention by which feature?
options: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
originalOptions: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Painless, palpable, and percussible bladder
allQuestions.explanation: Chronic retention classically presents as a painless, palpable/percussible bladder due to gradual distension, in contrast to the painful presentation of acute retention.

allQuestions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic heart disease presents with fever of 40°C, HR 125, BP 120/65, and suprapubic tenderness consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis with urinary retention. The most appropriate management is:
options: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
originalOptions: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
allQuestions.explanation: In acute bacterial prostatitis, urethral catheterization and instrumentation are contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia; urinary retention should be managed with a suprapubic catheter along with IV antibiotics and admission.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following clinical situations requires urgent decompression of the urinary tract?
options: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
originalOptions: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) An obstructed, infected collecting system
allQuestions.explanation: An obstructed and infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urologic emergency requiring urgent decompression via JJ stent or nephrostomy to prevent sepsis and renal destruction.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of long-term double-J (JJ) ureteral stenting?
allQuestions.explanation: Long-standing catheters (not JJ stents specifically) are linked to stone formation and bladder cancer risk with prolonged indwelling urethral catheters; urothelial cancer is not a typical direct complication attributed to JJ stents, whose common complications are infection, hematuria, and irritative/positional flank pain.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medications used for overactive bladder?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, and confusion, due to inhibition of parasympathetic (muscarinic) activity on the gut and other organs.

allQuestions.text: A fetus is found to have antenatal hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound. Appropriate postnatal evaluation includes:
options: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
originalOptions: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
allQuestions.explanation: Postnatal workup of antenatal hydronephrosis is guided by severity, using renal ultrasound as the initial test, followed by VCUG (to assess for reflux) and/or renal scan (to assess function/obstruction) as indicated.

allQuestions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have mild hydronephrosis on ultrasound with no symptoms of infection or stone disease. This is most likely explained by:
options: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
originalOptions: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
allQuestions.explanation: Mild hydronephrosis in pregnancy, particularly on the right side, is commonly physiological due to compression of the ureter by the enlarging gravid uterus and does not necessarily indicate pathology.

allQuestions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ER after a motorcycle accident with a deceleration mechanism. He has flank ecchymosis and gross hematuria. What is the single best indicator of significant renal injury in this patient?
allQuestions.explanation: Hematuria is the best indicator of significant renal injury, though its degree does not correlate reliably with injury severity, so imaging decisions are not based on hematuria grade alone.

allQuestions.text: A 40-year-old man sustains a stab wound to the flank. Compared to blunt renal trauma, penetrating renal trauma is characterized by:
options: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
Lower likelihood of requiring surgical intervention
originalOptions: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
Lower likelihood of requiring surgical intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Higher percentage of complications and need for surgical intervention
allQuestions.explanation: Penetrating trauma (gunshot/stab) causes a higher rate of complications and more often requires surgical intervention than blunt trauma.

allQuestions.text: Which finding is most specifically associated with reno-vascular (pedicle) injury after blunt trauma?
allQuestions.explanation: Significant deceleration causes tearing at points of fixation such as the renal hilum, making this the key historical clue for vascular injury.

allQuestions.text: A hemodynamically stable adult sustains blunt abdominal trauma with one documented episode of hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) and microscopic hematuria. Renal imaging is indicated because:
options: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
All blunt trauma requires imaging regardless of findings
Imaging is never needed if hematuria is microscopic
Imaging is reserved for penetrating trauma only
originalOptions: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
All blunt trauma requires imaging regardless of findings
Imaging is never needed if hematuria is microscopic
Imaging is reserved for penetrating trauma only
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Microscopic hematuria with an episode of hypotension is an indication for imaging
allQuestions.explanation: Blunt trauma with microscopic hematuria plus even one episode of hypotension (SBP <90) is a specific indication for renal imaging, unlike simple stable microscopic hematuria.

allQuestions.text: The gold standard imaging modality for suspected renal trauma is:
allQuestions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for renal trauma, allowing grading of injury and assessment of associated structures (hilum, perinephric space, vena cava).

allQuestions.text: One-shot intraoperative IVP performed during renal trauma surgery is primarily used to:
options: Grade the degree of renal laceration
Assess function of the contralateral kidney
originalOptions: Grade the degree of renal laceration
Assess function of the contralateral kidney
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Assess function of the contralateral kidney
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Assess function of the contralateral kidney
allQuestions.explanation: The one-shot IVP (10 minutes after IV contrast push) is mainly used intraoperatively to confirm that the contralateral kidney is functioning before proceeding with nephrectomy if needed.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the primary criterion guiding management of renal trauma?
options: Presence of gross vs microscopic hematuria
originalOptions: Presence of gross vs microscopic hematuria
allQuestions.explanation: Hemodynamic stability is the primary criterion determining management; stable patients are typically managed conservatively regardless of imaging grade, unstable patients require intervention.

allQuestions.text: Selective angio-embolization is most indicated in renal trauma when CT shows:
options: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
originalOptions: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Contrast leak, AV fistula, or aneurysm
allQuestions.explanation: CT findings of active contrast extravasation, arteriovenous fistula, or aneurysm are indications for selective angio-embolization.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an indication for renal exploration after trauma?
options: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
Stable patient with contrast leak amenable to embolization
originalOptions: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
Stable patient with contrast leak amenable to embolization
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma found at laparotomy
allQuestions.explanation: An expanding or pulsatile perirenal hematoma discovered at laparotomy, along with non-response to resuscitation, grade 5 vascular injury, or failed embolization, are indications for surgical exploration.

allQuestions.text: A patient with pelvic fracture and gross hematuria is suspected of having a bladder injury. Which imaging study should be performed to exclude bladder rupture?
allQuestions.explanation: Any patient with pelvic fracture and gross (visible) hematuria should undergo cystography to exclude bladder rupture, as visible hematuria is the principal sign of bladder trauma.

allQuestions.text: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture most commonly results from:
options: A sudden blow to a distended bladder
Spontaneous rupture in a healthy bladder
originalOptions: A sudden blow to a distended bladder
Spontaneous rupture in a healthy bladder
allQuestions.explanation: Extraperitoneal bladder injury is almost always secondary to pelvic fracture, whereas intraperitoneal rupture typically results from a blow to a distended bladder raising intravesical pressure.

allQuestions.text: On cystography, intraperitoneal bladder rupture is classically identified by:
options: Flame-shaped extravasation in perivesical soft tissue
Contrast pooling only within the bladder lumen
Extravasation limited to the prostatic urethra
originalOptions: Flame-shaped extravasation in perivesical soft tissue
Contrast pooling only within the bladder lumen
Extravasation limited to the prostatic urethra
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Contrast leak outlining bowel loops
allQuestions.explanation: Intraperitoneal rupture shows contrast outlining bowel loops as it leaks into the peritoneal cavity, while extraperitoneal rupture shows a flame-shaped perivesical extravasation pattern.

allQuestions.text: Management of an isolated extraperitoneal bladder rupture without bladder neck involvement is:
options: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
originalOptions: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Conservative management with Foley catheter drainage
allQuestions.explanation: Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture is managed conservatively with Foley catheter drainage; surgery is reserved for bladder neck involvement or associated injuries. Intraperitoneal rupture, in contrast, always requires surgical repair.

allQuestions.text: A man reports a popping sound during vigorous intercourse followed by immediate detumescence, pain, and eggplant-shaped swelling of the penis. Blood is noted at the urethral meatus. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Immediate surgical exploration without further workup
Blind Foley catheter placement to relieve retention
originalOptions: Immediate surgical exploration without further workup
Blind Foley catheter placement to relieve retention
allQuestions.explanation: Blood at the urethral meatus after suspected penile fracture indicates possible urethral injury; a retrograde urethrogram must be performed before attempting catheterization.

allQuestions.text: In penile fracture, the structure that must be surgically repaired is the:
allQuestions.explanation: Penile fracture is a tear of the tunica albuginea; surgical exploration, hematoma evacuation, and closure of this tear is the definitive management and reduces complications compared with conservative treatment.
